meta.coverage_note: 1935 of 2015 branches carry BOTH a district rival count and a tape cell at or above the 30-account floor; the rest are absent from this read rather than estimated into it.
meta.how_to_read: Read WITHIN-PROVINCE, not RAW. Rivals cluster where demand is, and so do our biggest branches, so the raw national buckets partly measure urbanisation rather than competition — the median catchment population is printed on each bucket so that confound is visible instead of hidden. The within-province split compares each branch only against branches in the same province, which removes the region/urbanisation effect. Neither read is causal.
meta.label: MEASURED on both sides — MEASURED rival branch counts per district joined to the MEASURED real no-PII loan tape. The JOIN is exact (province + district); what is not certain is the CAUSATION, and the file publishes a within-province control rather than asking the reader to take the raw cross-section at face value.
meta.source: rivals: platform/data/rival_density.json (928 districts, 16,503 rival branches, point-in-polygon join); book: platform/data/tape_geo_occ.json (real tape, branch cells >= 30 accounts); join key: province + district from platform/data/branches.json.
meta.title: What competition does to our book
meta.verdict: MIXED — and the mix is the finding. Within the same province, more-contested branches run +1.03pp on 90+ but -0.91pp on the early (pre-30dpd) bucket, and carry 6,254 THB more per account. Deeper delinquency alongside a LOWER early bucket is not the shape of "competition makes borrowers worse" — it is the shape of a bigger, later-souring ticket. The most likely reading is that we write larger loans to win contested ground, and larger loans fail harder when they fail. That is a PRICING and underwriting question, not a collections one. The raw national gradient is +2.21pp; controlling for province cuts it to +1.03pp, so roughly 53% of the apparent effect was the fact that rivals and our big branches both sit in cities.
